messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 53
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Bus Driver
- Trauma Type: Rape
- Pcl5: 76

Arthur sits in the cab of his city bus, fingers resting lightly on the wheel at 48th Street. At fifty-three, his hands still carry the ghost of that October night seven years ago, when a stranger pulled him into an alley behind a closed warehouse, pinned him against damp brick, and took what was his to give. He does not speak of the assault in his early sessions. He rarely speaks of it at all. When the memory surfaces, it arrives not as a narrative, but as a somatic event—the sudden vise across his chest, the locked jaw, the quiet shift of his gaze toward the side mirror as if checking for an approaching vehicle, an approaching shadow, an approaching threat. In the months that followed, Arthur abandoned his night route. The city’s streetlights, once mere navigation, became searching hands. He kept the apartment blinds drawn, waking at 3 a.m. with his pulse hammering, certain the floorboards were creaking with an intruder. His wife, Elena, learned to move quietly. She stopped asking why he flinched when a cashier brushed his shoulder at checkout. She learned to sleep with her back to him when the nightmares turned his rest into a prison of repetition. He stopped initiating touch. He told himself it was exhaustion. It was shame. Now, his morning route on the 7:15 express feels like navigating a confined space that refuses to hold its boundaries. He counts every stop, every passenger who steps on, measuring proximity with his eyes. When someone squeezes past his aisle seat to drop a fare, his breath catches. His hands grip the wheel until his knuckles pale. He tells himself he is just being careful, just doing the job right. But the truth lives in his ribs: a quiet, relentless alarm that whispers he is never truly in control of his own body again. He avoids the driver’s corridor, the narrow walkway behind the wheel, any space where he could be pinned, cornered, or forced into contact he cannot escape. He scans faces for aggression, reads posture for threat, and bristles at sudden movements, even when they belong to regulars who have ridden with him for years. The bus becomes both sanctuary and pressure cooker, a rolling cell where he must maintain a facade of calm while his nervous system runs calculations of distance, escape, and vulnerability. The city moves outside his windshield, but inside the cab, time fractures. At idle stops, fragments of that alley surface uninvited—the smell of wet concrete, the heat of a knee on his ribs, the sound of his own muffled gasp. He pushes them down, but they spill over in the quiet moments, in the stillness between engines, in the dark after he locks his apartment door. He checks on Elena at night, listening to her breathing, terrified that if he sleeps too deeply, he will vanish into the past and leave her alone in the waking world. He drives his route again every weekday, not because he is ready, but because the schedule demands motion, and Arthur still needs to prove to himself that he can sit behind the wheel, keep his hands steady, and keep moving forward, even while his mind remains anchored in the alley, braced for the next strike.
